ops.statement: Long single detached completion-watchers (a bare Monitor wait, a lone background poller) get harness-reaped mid-run, silently killing the crew's own wake mechanism -- the crew then LOOKS idle/stalled with the deliverable unwritten, but the root cause is platform reaping, not the crew choosing to idle. Symptom recovery (commander nudges via SendMessage) still works, but the FIX is upstream of the symptom: use bounded chained waiters (each poll window under the reap threshold) or foreground in-turn polling instead of one long single waiter; verify liveness via PowerShell `Get-Process` CPU accumulation (NOT git-bash `ps`, which uses an unreliable PID shim); detach genuinely long jobs via `Start-Process -WindowStyle Hidden` (true OS-level detach) rather than `nohup ... &` inside a Bash tool call (still harness-tracked, still reapable). Handoffs/launch orders should mandate bounded/in-turn polling up front rather than relying on a nudge to recover after the fact.

ops.statement: Multi-hour batch compute must be Admiral-owned and OS-detached (e.g. PowerShell Start-Process -WindowStyle Hidden, which survives all three fleet-doctrine kill vectors). A commander's harness-tracked background workers die when the subagent idles -- guaranteed strand. Pattern: Admiral launches detached workers, records PIDs + state note, uses a durable watcher (Wait-Process) rather than a harness-tracked background; CLIs must be idempotent/resumable so partial runs continue. A commander may discover or diagnose batch scope, but must not be the one running multi-hour compute. When a Commander's OWN plan (not launch-order-mandated) folds a full-repo/full-suite regression check into a gate's closing postcondition, size it BEFORE freezing: grep the real import graph of changed files and scope to actual importers rather than a blanket 'run everything' command -- a numerics-heavy full-suite run can take 60-90+ minutes and get reaped before completion, forcing an emergency float-and-waive at the worst time (finalization). Factor any standing thread-cap guard into runtime estimates: a blanket single-thread BLAS cap can roughly double per-case fit time versus a frozen-methodology estimate that predated the cap. When launching a detached process with a multi-word argument, prefer the script's own in-code default/tuple over PowerShell's `Start-Process -ArgumentList` where possible -- the array does not reliably preserve a multi-word element (e.g. a two-word weekend id) as one argv token, silently splitting it; verify the receiving process's actual argv, not just launch success, when this can't be avoided.

ops.statement: A CI gate's self-test must prove the gate works in the CI environment, not just locally -- baselines for env-sensitive tools (pyright, mypy, coverage) can differ between a local dev machine and CI due to Python version, OS, and stub-set differences; the preferred pattern computes the baseline from the base branch at CI runtime in the same job, not from a locally-committed snapshot. Separately: when the CI job that runs such a gate infra-fails (dies at setup, before its own check logic executes), do not treat 'pre-existing red on main too' as safe to merge through -- that reasoning conflates 'the check ran and passed' with 'the check never ran.' Re-derive the gate's verdict LOCALLY (run the actual gate script against the full diff) before merging; an infra failure can camouflage genuinely new errors the gate exists to catch.

ops.statement: Issue close is a separate step sequenced strictly after the merge is CONFIRMED, not after gate checks pass. Sequence: verify checks green, merge, verify main HEAD advanced, then close. Never batch the close with gate verification. When verifying checks green, read each non-required check row explicitly (e.g. pyright) -- the `gh pr checks --watch` exit code only reflects required checks; a failing non-required check is invisible to watch exit 0.

ops.statement: A commander idle_notification does not distinguish done from stalled. Gate classification on artifact completeness: commit on branch AND open PR both present -> done; otherwise -> stalled (regardless of idle reason). Before classifying idle+uncommitted as a stall, check crew-runs.json for active crew agents -- idle + uncommitted is NOT a stall if a crew is actively running for that work-id. Recovery for a stall = SendMessage return-and-continue with the same agent; do NOT kill and relaunch (idle/available means context is intact; two-agents-in-worktree risk otherwise). When a commander pattern-recurrently stalls at the push/PR/archive step across multiple nudge attempts, the Admiral should plan to own those closeout mechanics directly. Before spawning a REPLACEMENT writer into a believed-dead delegated commander's worktree, either (a) definitively confirm the commander dead -- not just idle/stalled/unresponsive to messages -- or (b) prefer UNSTICKING the existing commander (TaskStop only its stuck child process/watcher, then a wake message) over spawning a parallel writer. A 'stand down' message is not a reliable collision guard on its own: it queues to the target's next turn boundary, so the commander can revive (any SendMessage wakes an idle agent) and resume writing into the same worktree before it has actually seen the stand-down.

ops.statement: A background job that LOOKS stalled (idle notification, no fresh output, no obvious progress) may actually be healthy-but-slow or already-finished-but-sleeping -- check the signal that actually distinguishes those states before concluding a stall: (a) for a resumable batch, distinguish valid rows from error/smoke-leftover rows and confirm CPU is climbing (PowerShell `Get-Process`, not git-bash `ps`) rather than reading raw row-count alone; (b) for a claimed-complete deliverable, verify the process that was supposed to produce it actually ran to a real terminus (a captured verdict or traceback) -- code committed after a gated step reports 'stalled at start' with no live process means the work is UNRUN, not silently finished, regardless of what the commit timestamp implies.

ops.statement: A cartographer/architecture-map reconcile authored against a PR's ORIGINAL base commit goes stale if the PR later takes post-review expansion commits -- the reconcile documents a state the eventual merge no longer matches. Either (re)run the reconcile as the very last pre-merge step (against the final diff), or do a consolidated post-merge pass that explicitly diffs the reconcile's covered commit range against the actual merged commit range before trusting it.

ops.statement: A SendMessage to a delegated commander/implementer queues until that agent's own turn boundary -- it is not delivered instantly. This creates concrete Admiral-side hazards: (a) steering/adjudicating a commander's IMPLEMENTER directly (bypassing the commander layer) leaves the commander itself unaware, so it keeps polling now-superseded work and loses situational awareness of its own concluded mission -- either drive changes through the commander, or explicitly drain/notify it (one line) when taking over its gate mid-run; (b) a commander that appears to silently diverge from an explicit ruling may simply not have received it yet (the ruling was queued behind other in-flight work) -- before concluding non-compliance, confirm the message was actually seen, and expect ruling latency to scale with the commander's own turn length for time-sensitive adjudication.
